newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK Conservative supporters seen abstaining.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK Conservative supporters seen abstaining.

text.p: Some of Britain's ruling Conservative party's traditional supporters will stay away from the polling booth on May 1, causing a slight drop in the overall turnout, a Reuters survey of experts published on Wednesday showed.

The median of 20 forecasts from a panel of leading experts in voting patterns, collected on Tuesday, showed that 75 percent of the eligible population would vote, giving the opposition Labour party a majority of 77 seats.
At the last election in 1992, 77.8 percent of the 43.98 million people eligible to vote went to the polls.

Allegations of sex scandals, corruption and incompetence have beset the 18-year-old Conservative government, detracting from issues of economic competence which Prime Minister John Major has sought to highlight.
Some of the the traditional Conservative base, disillusioned by the seemingly endless series of scandals, will solve their dilemma by abstaining, experts said.
"The turnout will be lower among Conservative voters. They are unhappy with their party and will simply sit this one out," said Michael Thrasher, reader in politics at the University of Plymouth.

Most of the experts said the lower turnout would have only a marginal effect on the overall result, as Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system would not alter the outcome in safe Conservative seats.

"Historically where a clear winner is emerging, the turnout in the polls hasn't really changed the result. And the outcome of this election is inevitable," said Paul Whitely, professor of politics at the University of Sheffield.
But David Carlton, lecturer in politics at the University of Warwick, went against the majority of the experts by saying a low turnout would benefit the Conservatives.

"If there is an 80 percent turnout in the general election that would undoubtedly favour Labour but if it is as low as 70 percent then Labour's apparent lead in the poll might begin to ebb away," said Carlton, who expects a 70 percent turnout.
Carlton last month changed his prediction to a hung parliament from a Conservative majority of nine.
The highest forecast for the turnout, at 81 percent, was made by Justin Fisher, lecturer at London Guildhall University.

"The turnout will be higher than last time because it is an exciting election -- there is a real prospect of change. Labour voters who wouldn't normally bother will vote because they want to ensure their party gets in," said Fisher.
